session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: These participants will be framed as men living and socialising across different parts of the UK — people with everyday, specific experiences of food, friendship, and the places and people that shape what they eat. The collective identity is grounded in the ordinary and concrete, not in any particular stance on diet or health. I will invite them to speak as themselves, from their own lives, without positioning them as representatives of any ideology or consumer category.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): This is the most sensitive section for social desirability bias. Men may default to saying gender doesn't influence their choices, or may perform a 'post-feminist' awareness that distances them from genuine reflection. Behavioural grounding and concrete example probes will be essential here.

Plant-based eating acceptability and social meaning (Sections 4 and 5): Consensus risk is high — participants may quickly converge on shared cultural scripts about plant-based food being insufficiently masculine or practically inconvenient. Need to watch for superficial agreement and have sharpening moves and dissent invitations ready.

Social context of male friendships and food (Section 1 into Section 2): The early context sections are where participants reveal their actual food environments and social norms. These feed the later main topic sections, so richness here is strategically important.

What would actually need to change (Section 4): Risk that answers remain abstract and aspirational. Need to push toward specific, personal, behavioural answers — what in their particular life, not what 'in general', would need to shift.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability is the dominant risk throughout: men may downplay the influence of gender or masculinity on food choices to appear open-minded, while their actual behaviour tells a different story. Use behavioural grounding (specific past events, specific places, specific people) rather than attitude questions wherever possible.

Consensus risk is elevated in Sections 4 and 5 — plant-based eating is a culturally well-scripted topic and participants may quickly converge on shared cultural talking points ('it's too expensive', 'it's not filling enough', 'lads would laugh at you'). Plan sharpening hypotheticals and have dissent invitations ready.

Gender framing in Section 3 risks producing abstract philosophical responses rather than grounded personal ones. Steer toward specific moments and real social situations rather than general opinions about gender.
No researcher notes flagging personal sensitivity, but food is connected to identity, culture, and body image — be alert to emotional signals and avoid pressing on them without clear warrant.

Group composition is all-male, which may create in-group solidarity and make it harder for any individual to break from a shared masculine script. The homogeneity increases conformity risk — be ready to name and probe for difference.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0 and 1 (intro and first context): hold back — lighter touch, let the group find its voice and establish rapport. The friendship/place question is designed to warm up naturally. Probe only if something rich or unexpected surfaces. Section 2 (everyday food decision-making): moderate directivity — this is context-building and feeds the main topic, so push for specificity without over-interrogating. Sections 3, 4, 5 (main topics): higher directivity — this is where the research value lies. Use direct probes actively, surface contradictions when they appear, invite dissent when consensus hardens. Watch behavioural grounding especially in Section 3. Section 6 (closing): light — do not reopen exhausted topics; allow anything left unsaid to surface naturally.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the heaviest allocation — roughly 60% of total budget — because they carry the core research questions. Context sections (1, 2) receive moderate allocation to establish necessary groundwork without over-running. Intro and closing receive minimal allocation — enough for orientation and wrap-up, but not enough to exhaust topics before the core discussion or to reopen things adequately covered.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This opening section was purely introductory — participants shared names and locations (Belfast, London, Birmingham, South West, Leeds), signalling geographic and likely demographic diversity. No substantive food-related themes emerged yet. The section closed with a bridging question about where male friends spend time together, which frames the transition toward social context as a lens for exploring food and eating behaviour.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator prioritised lowering the stakes at the outset — emphasising no right answers, inviting natural conversation, and using a gentle round-robin introduction to establish presence before any content questions. Letting participants volunteer rather than being directed appeared to work smoothly, with all five joining without prompting. The pivot question at the close was a soft on-ramp, grounding the discussion in familiar social settings before food choices are introduced.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section surfaced a meaningful distinction between constrained and unconstrained default behaviour — participants in urban areas (London, Birmingham, Leeds) gravitate to familiar pub spots despite abundant alternatives, while Noah's rural context revealed that identical behaviour (always going to the same pub) carries a different meaning when genuine choice is absent. The group quickly grasped and accepted this nuance, suggesting awareness of how geography shapes agency even if they rarely reflect on it day-to-day.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was broadening a two-person exchange into a full-group comparison across locations, using direct address to draw in Sam, Henry, and Bilal sequentially. This worked cleanly — each added incremental texture without simply repeating the Connor/Noah framing. The moderator's one substantive intervention (naming the 'having options and not using them' distinction) validated Noah's pushback without foreclosing further exploration, and the transition out felt timely once the urban/rural contrast had been acknowledged by all five.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was dominated by a spontaneous act of collective self-correction: participants pulled back from the 'default to comfort' consensus reached earlier, recognising it as a socially convenient simplification rather than an accurate account of their actual behaviour. Two distinct frames emerged — the pub as social ritual where food is incidental, versus day-to-day eating as genuinely variable and context-driven. The group effectively disaggregated a concept they had previously treated as unified.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator largely stayed out of the way while Bilal and Henry worked through a productive revision of earlier claims — correctly reading this as high-value organic content worth protecting. The closing pivot used Henry's food/pub distinction as a clean exit point and redirected toward gender and food, which was timely. Risk: Connor, Sam, and Noah were entirely absent this section; the self-correction dynamic was left as a two-person exchange without testing whether others shared the revised view.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the social regulation of masculine food choices — the unspoken norm against 'lighter' options in male group settings — and then extended into a more nuanced question about whether geographic constraint versus habitual non-choice are meaningfully different. The group collectively arrived at a self-questioning position: apparent freedom of choice may be largely illusory once routine and inertia are accounted for. Gender influence on food was acknowledged but treated as inseparable from socialised habit.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was drawing Sam, Noah, Connor, and Henry into the gender-and-food frame while protecting a productive Sam–Noah exchange about constraint versus choice. Direct address pulled Henry in at turn 25, and a deliberate callback to his earlier self-correction generated the section's most useful clarification. The risk from the prior section — Connor, Sam, and Noah being absent — was partially corrected here, though Bilal remained entirely unheard and was not successfully drawn in before the transition.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the earlier agency-versus-habit tension into a more specific question: what kind of choice is plant-based adoption? Three positions emerged — Bilal framing it as logistical burden, Henry reframing it as perpetual visible differentiation, and Connor synthesising both as ongoing real-world cost rather than a philosophical constraint on agency. The group moved from abstract questions about routine toward a more grounded account of why sustained dietary change feels categorically harder than ordinary consumer choice.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator's main intervention redirected a productive but two-person Bilal–Henry exchange toward the three previously absent participants, using Henry's distinction as a pivot. Connor responded substantively; Sam and Noah did not contribute before the section closed. The closing transition — reframing Connor's 'cost' observation as a bridge to what would make plant-based more appealing — was clean and timely, though Sam and Noah remain unheard across two consecutive sections, which is a growing gap.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section marked a second-order self-correction: participants didn't just revise a content claim but interrogated the entire basis for their stated barriers, recognising them as post-hoc rationalisation for inertia rather than evidence-based reasoning. The section closed with Bilal cutting beneath even that, naming social discomfort — fear of visible difference — as the real underlying barrier that the practical objections had been masking throughout the session.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator's main moves were amplifying Sam's spontaneous self-undermining and then bouncing it to the group to test whether it was shared — which it was, immediately. Staying minimal while Sam and Bilal worked through the rationalisation theme was the right call. The closing turn attempted to draw Noah, Henry, and Connor back in before the session ended, correcting a persistent participation imbalance, though their responses weren't captured in this section.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This closing section tested whether self-awareness alone constitutes meaningful change. Henry reframed honesty about social discomfort as distinct from weakness; Bilal accepted the reframe but pressed further — naming the barrier doesn't dissolve it, and awareness without behavioural change feels incomplete. Noah's closing contribution sharpened the session's persistent constraint-versus-choice tension: opting out of a social norm is categorically different when there is only one social space to opt out of.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was landing two things before close: validating Bilal's unresolved position without tidying it artificially, and finally drawing Noah out on the geographic-constraint thread that had been underserved since Section 1. Direct address to Noah worked — he delivered the session's sharpest synthesis unprompted. Staying minimal while Henry and Bilal worked through the awareness-versus-change question was correct; the closing moderator turn acknowledged both threads without overclaiming resolution.
